title: Photosensitivity and Photodermatoses -- Continuing Education Activity
content: Photosensitivity disorders comprise a diverse group of conditions in which ultraviolet radiation or visible light induces or worsens cutaneous disease, creating frequent diagnostic and management dilemmas in dermatologic practice. Photodistributed eruptions may reflect idiopathic photodermatoses, exogenous photosensitizer reactions, endogenous photosensitizer disorders, photoexacerbated dermatoses, or photosensitive genodermatoses, and the correct category drives testing and treatment. Drug- and chemical-induced photosensitivity is common and may be phototoxic or photoallergic, often involving ultraviolet A (UVA) action spectra, and can be missed if clinicians do not systematically review exposures and morphology. Photosensitivity in connective tissue disease and porphyrias can carry systemic implications, so a structured approach is essential to avoid delayed diagnosis.

title: Photosensitivity and Photodermatoses -- Continuing Education Activity
content: This educational activity provides a framework for recognizing, classifying, evaluating, and managing photosensitive eruptions using evidence-based strategies and guideline-informed testing where applicable. Participants review clinical patterns, diagnostic phototesting concepts, targeted laboratory evaluation, and practical photoprotection strategies, including approaches relevant to UVA and visible light. The course emphasizes how coordinated interprofessional care among dermatologists, primary care clinicians, nurses, and pharmacists improves medication reconciliation, patient counseling, adherence to photoprotection, and safe long-term disease control.

title: Photosensitivity and Photodermatoses -- Continuing Education Activity
content: Objectives: Differentiate phototoxic, photoallergic, and immune-mediated photosensitivity using timing, morphology, and exposure history. Identify medications and chemical agents commonly associated with phototoxic and photoallergic reactions. Select appropriate treatment regimens for systemic and genetic disorders associated with photosensitivity. Collaborate effectively with an interprofessional healthcare team, including nurses, pharmacists, and other health professionals, to counsel patients with photosensitivity on appropriate sun protection. Access free multiple choice questions on this topic.

title: Photosensitivity and Photodermatoses -- Introduction
content: Photosensitivity refers to an abnormal cutaneous response to ultraviolet (UV) radiation or visible light and encompasses a broad spectrum of disorders with distinct mechanisms and clinical implications. [1] A practical clinical framework classifies photodermatoses into 5 major categories: Idiopathic photodermatoses Exogenous-agent photodermatoses Endogenous-agent photodermatoses (notably porphyrias) Photoexacerbated dermatoses Photosensitive genodermatoses [1]

title: Photosensitivity and Photodermatoses -- Introduction
content: Many conditions are triggered primarily by ultraviolet A (UVA), which penetrates deeper into the skin and through window glass, whereas visible-light–driven disease is especially relevant in pigmentary disorders and certain photosensitive dermatoses, requiring tinted/iron-oxide strategies. [2] Tinted sunscreens can be particularly beneficial for visible-light–associated photodermatoses because they can improve spectral coverage that conventional UV filters do not fully address. [3]

title: Photosensitivity and Photodermatoses -- Introduction
content: Photosensitivity may be episodic and benign (eg, seasonal idiopathic photodermatoses) or may signal risk of systemic disease (eg, systemic lupus erythematosus photosensitivity) and metabolic disorders (eg, porphyrias). Therefore, careful classification and evaluation are central to patient safety. [4] In systemic lupus erythematosus, abnormal reactivity to both UV radiation and visible light can be observed during phototesting, supporting the clinical relevance of broader-spectrum avoidance and protection strategies in selected patients. [5]

title: Photosensitivity and Photodermatoses -- Etiology
content: Etiologies of photosensitivity vary by category and include immune-mediated hypersensitivity, direct phototoxic injury, endogenous photosensitizer accumulation, and inherited defects in DNA repair. [1] Exogenous photosensitivity arises from medications, topical agents, or plant-derived compounds that absorb light and cause tissue injury (phototoxicity) or immune-mediated dermatitis (photoallergy), with many clinically important agents acting primarily in the UVA range. [6] Antimicrobials and other drug classes can provoke photosensitivity through phototoxic or photoallergic mechanisms, and distinguishing these pathways informs counseling, avoidance, and patch-testing or photopatch-testing strategies. [7]

title: Photosensitivity and Photodermatoses -- Etiology
content: Endogenous photosensitizers are central to porphyrias, in which accumulation of porphyrin pathway intermediates drives either bullous skin fragility syndromes or nonbullous, painful photosensitivity phenotypes, necessitating targeted biochemical testing rather than broad autoimmune panels. [8] Reviews of acute and cutaneous porphyrias emphasize that cutaneous disease results from porphyrin-induced photosensitivity and may coexist with neurovisceral attacks depending on the subtype. [9] Contemporary clinical updates underscore that several porphyrias can present with photosensitivity and that diagnosis relies on measurement of characteristic porphyrin or precursor patterns. [10] Photosensitive genodermatoses include xeroderma pigmentosum, in which defective nucleotide excision repair results in extreme UV sensitivity and a markedly increased risk of skin cancer, making early recognition and rigorous photoprotection essential. [11]

title: Photosensitivity and Photodermatoses -- Epidemiology
content: Photosensitivity disorders occur worldwide and affect individuals of all ages, sexes, and ethnic backgrounds, although the prevalence and distribution of specific photodermatoses vary considerably across geographic locations, genetic backgrounds, and environmental exposure patterns. [1] Idiopathic photodermatoses, particularly polymorphic light eruption, represent the most common category and are reported most frequently in temperate climates and higher latitudes, where intermittent sun exposure predominates. [12] Sex differences are evident in several photosensitivity disorders, with a female predominance observed in polymorphic light eruption and autoimmune photoexacerbated dermatoses such as cutaneous lupus erythematosus. [13] In contrast, genetic photodermatoses such as xeroderma pigmentosum affect men and women equally and often present in early childhood. [11]

title: Photosensitivity and Photodermatoses -- Epidemiology
content: Age at presentation varies by disease category, with idiopathic photodermatoses often beginning in adolescence or early adulthood, photoexacerbated connective tissue diseases typically presenting in adulthood, and inherited disorders manifesting in infancy or early childhood. [1] Drug-induced photosensitivity may occur at any age and is influenced by prescribing patterns and comorbid disease burden. [6] Environmental factors such as latitude, altitude, season, and occupational sun exposure significantly influence disease expression, with higher UV intensity associated with earlier onset, greater severity, and more extensive anatomic involvement. [14] These epidemiologic patterns underscore the importance of individualized risk assessment when evaluating patients with suspected photosensitivity. [1]

title: Photosensitivity and Photodermatoses -- Pathophysiology
content: Photosensitivity results from an abnormal cutaneous response to electromagnetic radiation interacting with a skin chromophore, leading to cellular injury, immune activation, or both. [15] The most commonly implicated wavelengths are UVA, ultraviolet B, and visible light, with UVA responsible for the majority of acquired photosensitivity reactions due to its deeper dermal penetration and ability to pass through window glass. [16] [17] In immune-mediated photodermatoses, ultraviolet radiation induces the formation of photoantigens that trigger delayed hypersensitivity reactions through T-cell activation, cytokine release, and impaired ultraviolet radiation–induced immune suppression. [13] Regulatory T-cell dysfunction and altered antigen presentation have been implicated in sustaining these abnormal inflammatory responses. [18]

title: Photosensitivity and Photodermatoses -- Pathophysiology
content: Phototoxic reactions occur when an exogenous or endogenous photosensitizer absorbs light energy, generating reactive oxygen species that cause direct cellular damage without immune mediation. [6] In contrast, photoallergic reactions involve a type IV hypersensitivity response in which a light-altered compound acts as a hapten and elicits an immune response upon re-exposure. [7] In metabolic photodermatoses, such as porphyrias, accumulation of porphyrins in the skin facilitates energy transfer upon light exposure, resulting in tissue injury, vascular damage, and inflammation. [8]

title: Photosensitivity and Photodermatoses -- Pathophysiology
content: Other metabolic photodermatoses may result from nutritional deficiencies, such as pellagra, in which reactive oxygen species predominate in the absence of protective nutritional factors, leading to photodermatosis (see Image. Pellagra Photosensitivity). [19] [20] [21] The mechanism of photosensitivity in pellagra remains incompletely understood and may involve multiple pathways, including decreased urocanic acid levels, altered prostaglandin synthesis, and accumulation of porphyrins. [22] [23] Genetic photodermatoses arise from defects in DNA repair pathways, leading to the accumulation of UV-induced DNA damage and extreme photosensitivity, with a risk of malignant transformation. [11] Please see StatPearls' companion resource, " Niacin Deficiency ," for further information.

title: Photosensitivity and Photodermatoses -- Histopathology
content: Histopathologic findings in photosensitivity disorders vary widely depending on the underlying category and specific diagnosis, and no single pattern is pathognomonic across all photodermatoses. [1] In idiopathic photodermatoses such as polymorphic light eruption, histology typically demonstrates superficial and deep perivascular lymphocytic infiltrates, papillary dermal edema, and occasional spongiosis, without evidence of vasculitis. [24] [25] [26] Photoallergic dermatitis shares features with allergic contact dermatitis, including spongiosis and a lymphocytic infiltrate, while phototoxic reactions more closely resemble exaggerated sunburn with keratinocyte necrosis and epidermal damage. [6] In photoexacerbated autoimmune dermatoses such as cutaneous lupus erythematosus, interface dermatitis with basal vacuolar change, apoptotic keratinocytes, and dermal mucin deposition may be present. [4]

title: Photosensitivity and Photodermatoses -- Histopathology
content: Metabolic photodermatoses demonstrate distinctive histopathologic patterns, with porphyria cutanea tarda showing subepidermal blistering, festooning of dermal papillae, and deposition of periodic acid–Schiff–positive material around dermal vessels. [9] Genetic photosensitivity syndromes, such as xeroderma pigmentosum, may show nonspecific changes early but ultimately are characterized by actinic damage and multiple cutaneous cancers. [11] Because histopathologic findings often overlap, biopsy results must be interpreted in conjunction with clinical features, exposure history, and laboratory data to reach an accurate diagnosis. [1]

title: Photosensitivity and Photodermatoses -- History and Physical
content: A meticulous history and physical examination are the cornerstone of diagnosing photosensitivity disorders and frequently allow accurate classification before ancillary testing is pursued. [1] The clinical history should focus on the temporal relationship between light exposure and symptom onset, the reproducibility of eruptions, seasonal variation, and the duration of lesions after cessation of exposure. [15] Timing of eruption onset following exposure provides critical diagnostic clues; immediate reactions within minutes suggest solar urticaria, while delayed reactions developing hours to days later are characteristic of idiopathic photodermatoses such as polymorphic light eruption or photoallergic reactions. [13] Chronic, persistent eruptions with minimal seasonal variation raise suspicion for photoexacerbated dermatoses, including cutaneous lupus erythematosus or chronic actinic dermatitis. [4]

title: Photosensitivity and Photodermatoses -- History and Physical
content: Anatomic distribution is equally informative, as photosensitive eruptions typically involve sun-exposed areas such as the face, neck, the V of the chest, dorsal forearms, and hands, with relative sparing of skin protected by clothing. (See Image . Photosensitive Dermatitis.) [1] Sharp demarcation lines at clothing edges, jewelry, watchbands, or hairlines strongly support a photodistributed process. [15] Conversely, sparing of habitually sun-exposed areas, such as the face in polymorphic light eruption, reflects photohardening and is a distinguishing feature. [13]

title: Photosensitivity and Photodermatoses -- History and Physical
content: Morphologic characteristics vary widely across photodermatoses and must be carefully documented. [1] Papules, plaques, vesicles, and prurigo-like nodules are typical of idiopathic photodermatoses, while urticarial wheals suggest solar urticaria and eczematous plaques favor photoallergic or chronic actinic dermatitis. [6] Annular plaques that worsen with sun exposure are characteristic of subacute cutaneous lupus erythematosus. Bullae, skin fragility, and scarring on sun-exposed skin raise concern for porphyrias, particularly porphyria cutanea tarda. [9] Please see StatPearls' companion resource, " Porphyria Cutanea Tarda ," for more information.

title: Photosensitivity and Photodermatoses -- History and Physical
content: Medication and exposure history are essential because drug-induced photosensitivity remains a common and underrecognized cause of photodistributed eruptions. [6] A thorough review should include prescription medications, over-the-counter drugs, herbal supplements, topical agents, fragrances, and occupational or recreational exposures to plants and chemicals. [7] Common medications implicated in drug-induced photosensitivity include thiazide diuretics and doxycycline. The distinction between phototoxic and photoallergic reactions can often be inferred from dose, latency, and distribution. [6]

title: Photosensitivity and Photodermatoses -- History and Physical
content: Systemic symptoms and extracutaneous findings should be actively sought because photosensitivity may be a cutaneous manifestation of systemic disease. [4] Arthralgias, oral ulcers, Raynaud phenomenon, or fatigue may suggest connective tissue disease, while abdominal pain, neuropathy, or dark urine may indicate acute porphyria. [8] In children, growth delay, neurologic abnormalities, or early malignant neoplasms should prompt consideration of photosensitive genodermatoses. [11] Physical examination should extend beyond the skin to include the scalp, nails, mucous membranes, and signs of systemic disease. [1] Nailfold capillary abnormalities may support dermatomyositis, while poikiloderma and actinic damage may indicate chronic photosensitivity or genodermatoses. [15]

title: Photosensitivity and Photodermatoses -- Evaluation
content: The evaluation of photosensitivity disorders is guided by clinical suspicion and should be tailored to the most likely diagnosis. [1] National and international expert consensus emphasizes a stepwise approach beginning with history and physical examination, followed by targeted laboratory, photobiologic, and histopathologic testing when indicated. [27] Phototesting is a specialized diagnostic tool available in select centers and can aid in defining action spectra and reproducing disease. [15]

title: Photosensitivity and Photodermatoses -- Evaluation
content: Minimal erythema dose testing using broadband or monochromator systems can identify abnormal sensitivity to UVA or UVB and help distinguish idiopathic photodermatoses from normal skin responses. [28] [29] [30] Provocative phototesting with repeated UVA or UVB exposures over several days may reproduce lesions in polymorphic light eruption or chronic actinic dermatitis, but has variable sensitivity and a high false-negative rate. [31] Photopatch testing is indicated when photoallergic contact dermatitis is suspected and should be performed in conjunction with standard patch testing to identify allergens that require light activation. [7] European and British photodermatology guidelines recommend photopatch testing in patients with eczematous photodistributed eruptions and relevant exposure histories. [32] [33] [34]

title: Photosensitivity and Photodermatoses -- Evaluation
content: Laboratory evaluation should be selective and hypothesis-driven. [1] Antinuclear antibody testing and extractable nuclear antigen panels are appropriate when connective tissue disease is suspected, but are not recommended for routine screening in classic idiopathic photodermatoses. [4] Porphyrin studies in blood, urine, and stool are essential when blistering or painful photosensitivity suggests porphyria. [8]

title: Photosensitivity and Photodermatoses -- Evaluation
content: Skin biopsy with routine histopathology and direct immunofluorescence may help differentiate photoexacerbated autoimmune disease, chronic actinic dermatitis, and idiopathic photodermatoses when clinical features overlap. [35] [36] However, biopsy findings are often nonspecific and must be interpreted in the clinical context. [1] In suspected photosensitive genodermatoses, specialized testing such as post-UV cell survival assays, DNA repair studies, or targeted genetic sequencing may be required and should be coordinated through specialized centers. [11] Early identification is critical due to the markedly increased risk of skin cancer and the need for intensive surveillance. [11]

title: Photosensitivity and Photodermatoses -- Treatment / Management
content: Management of photosensitivity disorders centers on rigorous photoprotection combined with diagnosis-directed therapy for the underlying photodermatosis, as emphasized in contemporary reviews and evidence-based management frameworks for photodermatoses. [15] [37] Education on the specific wavelengths responsible for disease activity is essential because standard window glass blocks most UVB but transmits substantial UVA and visible light. [38] [39] Accordingly, many conventional sunscreens may provide insufficient UVA/visible-light attenuation unless high-UVA protection and tinted formulations are used. [3] [40]

title: Photosensitivity and Photodermatoses -- Treatment / Management
content: General photoprotective measures include avoidance of direct sunlight during peak hours, seeking shade, and minimizing exposure to artificial ultraviolet sources. [2] Protective clothing, including tightly woven fabrics, wide-brimmed hats, and garments labeled with ultraviolet protection factor, provides effective physical shielding and is emphasized in guideline recommendations. [2] Broad-spectrum sunscreens with high UVA protection should be applied generously and reapplied regularly, recognizing that the sun protection factor primarily indexes protection against erythemally effective solar UV that is largely confined to UVB and short-wavelength UVA. [41] [42] For disorders triggered or exacerbated by visible light, tinted sunscreens containing iron oxides may provide additional benefit and are increasingly recommended for selected photodermatoses. [3] Adjunctive strategies, including window films and laminated glass, may be appropriate for patients with severe or occupational photosensitivity. [2]

[3] Adjunctive strategies, including window films and laminated glass, may be appropriate for patients with severe or occupational photosensitivity. [2]

title: Photosensitivity and Photodermatoses -- Treatment / Management
content: Targeted therapies depend on the disease category. [1] Idiopathic photodermatoses, such as polymorphic light eruption, may benefit from controlled photohardening with narrowband UVB or PUVA under specialist supervision. [13] Drug-induced photosensitivity requires identification and discontinuation of the offending agent whenever feasible. [6] Photoexacerbated autoimmune dermatoses often require systemic immunomodulatory therapy in addition to strict photoprotection, guided by rheumatologic and dermatologic consensus recommendations. [4] For example, chronic actinic dermatitis (previously known as actinic reticuloid) may require immunosuppressive medications, such as azathioprine, if topical corticosteroids are ineffective.

title: Photosensitivity and Photodermatoses -- Treatment / Management
content: Porphyrias require disease-specific management, including avoidance of triggering drugs, treatment of iron overload when appropriate, and referral to specialized centers. [10] Genetic photosensitivity syndromes mandate lifelong photoprotection and intensive surveillance. [11] Small-molecule drugs targeting Janus kinase inhibitors are increasingly being studied for potential benefit in photodermatoses. [43] [44]

title: Photosensitivity and Photodermatoses -- Differential Diagnosis
content: The differential diagnosis of photosensitivity is broad and should consider the major photodermatosis categories. [1] Idiopathic photodermatoses (eg, polymorphous light eruption, actinic prurigo) must be distinguished from autoimmune photoexacerbated diseases (eg, cutaneous lupus erythematosus, dermatomyositis), metabolic disorders (eg, porphyrias, pellagra), drug-induced reactions (eg, methotrexate, doxycycline), and genetic syndromes (eg, xeroderma pigmentosum) based on history, morphology, and distribution. [15]

title: Photosensitivity and Photodermatoses -- Differential Diagnosis
content: Cutaneous lupus erythematosus is a key consideration in persistent photodistributed eruptions and may be distinguished by associated systemic features, serologic abnormalities, and characteristic histopathology. [4] Please see StatPearls' companion resource, " Systemic Lupus Erythematosus ," for further information.

content: Dermatomyositis should be considered when photosensitivity is accompanied by proximal muscle weakness or pathognomonic cutaneous signs such as Gottron papules. [45] Please see StatPearls' companion resource, " Dermatomyositis ," for more information.

title: Photosensitivity and Photodermatoses -- Prognosis
content: The prognosis of photosensitivity disorders varies widely according to etiology. [1] Idiopathic photodermatoses often follow a benign course, with many patients experiencing improvement over time or with appropriate photohardening strategies. [13] Photoexacerbated autoimmune disorders may have a chronic course and are influenced by the activity of the underlying systemic disease. [4] Metabolic photodermatoses require lifelong management, but outcomes have improved with earlier recognition and targeted therapy. [10] Genetic photosensitivity syndromes carry a guarded prognosis due to extreme cancer risk, although early diagnosis and strict photoprotection can improve survival. [11]

title: Photosensitivity and Photodermatoses -- Complications
content: Complications of photosensitivity disorders can include chronic actinic damage with pigmentary changes and photoaging. [47] In blistering photodermatoses, complications may include scarring and dyschromia, and erosions/bullae may require wound care to reduce the risk of secondary infection. [48] [49] Patients with genetic photosensitivity syndromes face a dramatically increased risk of nonmelanoma and melanoma skin cancers. [11] Psychosocial complications are common across disease categories and include anxiety, depression, social withdrawal, and reduced quality of life due to sun avoidance. [2] Excessive photoprotection and sun avoidance in patients with photosensitive disorders may contribute to vitamin D deficiency, necessitating monitoring and supplementation. [50]

title: Photosensitivity and Photodermatoses -- Deterrence and Patient Education
content: Patient education is central to the management of photosensitivity and should emphasize understanding disease triggers, proper photoprotection techniques, and realistic expectations regarding disease course. [2] Education on sunscreen selection, proper application (including sufficient coverage and minimizing missed areas), and reapplication timing improves protection and reduces preventable UV exposure in real-world use. [41] [51] [52] Patients should be counseled on lifestyle modifications, including travel planning, occupational adjustments, and the use of ultraviolet index resources and mobile applications. [2] Genetic counseling may be appropriate for inherited photosensitivity disorders. [11] Please see StatPearls' companion resource, " Sunscreens and Photoprotection ," for more information.

title: Photosensitivity and Photodermatoses -- Enhancing Healthcare Team Outcomes
content: Optimal management of photosensitivity disorders requires coordinated interprofessional care. [1] Dermatologists play a central role in diagnosis and management, while primary care clinicians assist with medication review and monitoring for systemic disease. [6] Nurses support patient education and adherence to photoprotection strategies, pharmacists identify photosensitizing medications and counsel on alternatives, and mental health professionals address psychosocial sequelae. [2] Effective communication and coordinated care enhance patient safety, satisfaction, and long-term outcomes across the spectrum of photosensitivity disorders.
